'''''Oenothera macrocarpa''''' ([[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Oenothera missouriensis''), the '''bigfruit evening primrose''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=OEMA|taxon=Oenothera macrocarpa|accessdate=29 January 2016}}</ref> '''Ozark sundrops''',<ref name = RHSPF/> '''Missouri evening primrose''',<ref name="natureserve">{{cite web |title=NatureServe Explorer 2.0 |url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.129287/Oenothera_macrocarpa |website=explorer.natureserve.org}}</ref> or '''Missouri primrose''',<ref name="AR">{{cite web |title=Oenothera macrocarpa; Missouri Primrose |url=https://www.uaex.uada.edu/yard-garden/resource-library/plant-week/Oenothera-macrocarpa-Missouri-Primrose-05-24-2019.aspx |website=Oenothera macrocarpa; Missouri Primrose |language=en}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the evening primrose [[family (botany)|family]] [[Onagraceae]], native to northeast [[Mexico]] and the south-central [[United States]], where it is found in [[calcareous]] prairies and limestone [[outcrop]]s.<ref name=brit>[http://www.brit.org/brit-press/nctexasflora/online Shinners and Mahler's Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas Online]</ref>

== Description ==
This [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] produces a red [[plant stem|stem]] up to {{convert |18|in|cm|0|order=flip|abbr=on|}} in height.<ref name="IL"/> The plant can sprawl along the ground up to {{convert |2|ft|m|1|order=flip|abbr=on|}}.<ref name="AR"/> Leaves are long and narrow, about {{convert |6|in|cm|0|order=flip|abbr=on|}} long by {{convert |1|in|cm|0|order=flip|abbr=on|}} across, and are densely crowded in an alternate arrangement along the stem.<ref name="IL">{{cite web |title=Missouri Evening Primrose (Oenothera macrocarpa) |url=https://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/prairie/plantx/ms_primrosex.htm |website=www.illinoiswildflowers.info}}</ref> They have either smooth margins or broadly spaced teeth and are hairy.<ref name="MP">{{cite web |title=Oenothera macrocarpa page |url=https://www.missouriplants.com/Oenothera_macrocarpa_page.html |website=www.missouriplants.com}}</ref>

The large flowers, up to {{convert |5|in|cm|0|order=flip|abbr=on|}} across, are cup shaped with four petals, canary yellow, and have a mild fragrance. They are produced in great numbers from early to mid summer. The flowers last for one day, opening in the evening and closing the following morning.<ref name="IL"/> Each flower has a very long [[floral tube]] {{cvt|10|–|11|cm}} in length,<ref>{{cite book | last1= Everard | first1= Barbara| last2= Morley | first2= Brian D. | date= 1970 | title= Wild Flowers of the World | location= New York | publisher= G.P. Putnam's Sons | page= Plate 156 }}</ref> The seed pods are 4-winged and {{convert |52-75|mm|in|0|abbr=on|}} long.<ref name="MP"/>

==Taxonomy==
There are five commonly accepted [[variety (botany)|varieties]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Oenothera macrocarpa Nutt. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:173157-2#children |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> These are: 
*''O. macrocarpa'' var. ''fremontii'' - restricted to [[Kansas]] and southern [[Nebraska]]<ref>{{PLANTS|id=oemaf|taxon=Oenothera macrocarpa|accessdate=18 January 2017}}</ref>
*''O. macrocarpa'' var. ''incana'' - southern Kansas, western [[Oklahoma]] and northern [[Texas]] 
*''O. macrocarpa'' var. ''macrocarpa'' - the most widespread; Texas to the [[Ozark Mountains]], with disjunct populations in Tennessee's [[Nashville Basin]]<ref name=chester>{{cite book |last=Chester |first=Edward |date=2015 |title=Guide to the Vascular Plants of Tennessee}}</ref>
*''O. macrocarpa'' var. ''mexicana'' - known only from [[Coahuila]], Mexico<ref>{{cite journal|jstor=i25027967|title=Revised Classification of the Onagraceae  |journal=Systematic Botany Monographs|volume=83 |first1=Warren|last1=Wagner|first2=Peter|last2=Hoch|first3=Peter|last3=Raven|date=2007}}</ref>
*''O. macrocarpa'' var. ''oklahomensis'' - southern Kansas, Oklahoma and northern Texas

==Etymology==
The genus name ''Oenothera'' is from the Greek for "wine-scented". The specific epithet ''macrocarpa'' is also from the Greek, meaning "large fruited".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Denison |first1=Edgar |title=Missouri Wildflowers |date=2017 |publisher=Conservation Commission of the State of Missouri |isbn=978-1-887247-59-7 |pages=137 |edition=Sixth}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Oenothera macrocarpa'' is native to Arkansas, Illinois, Kansas, Missouri, Nebraska, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Texas, and northeast Mexico.<ref>{{cite web |title=Oenothera macrocarpa Nutt. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:173157-2#distributions |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> Habitats include limestone outcrops, glades, bluffs, rocky prairies, quarries, and roadsides.<ref name="MP"/>

==Ecology==
The flowers are pollinated by night-flying moths, such as sphinx moths (''[[Sphingidae]]'').<ref name="IL"/> 

==Uses==
The seed pods are often used in [[Floral design|flower arrangements]]. This plant is also grown in gardens for its flowers.<ref name="MO">[http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/gardens-gardening/your-garden/plant-finder/plant-details/kc/e390/oenothera-macrocarpa.aspx Missouri Botanical Garden]</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.perennialresource.com/plants/general-perennial/643_oenothera-missouriensis.aspx |title=Perennial Resource: Oenothera missouriensis |access-date=2011-03-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120317171948/http://www.perennialresource.com/plants/general-perennial/643_oenothera-missouriensis.aspx |archive-date=2012-03-17 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It is suitable as a groundcover in poor, stony soil which does not become waterlogged in winter, in full sun. It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/70730/i-Oenothera-macrocarpa-i/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Oenothera macrocarpa'' | accessdate= 14 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  
| url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017
